segs.text: Module four, objective two. Glomerular filtration, tubular secretion and tubular reabsorption. The amount of drug that ends up in the urine is the net result of three processes in the kidney's nephron: filtration, secretion and reabsorption. The first two add drug to the tubular lumen, the fluid space inside the kidney tubule. Reabsorption moves drug from the lumen back into the bloodstream.

card.m: urine: net of filtration, secretion, reabsorption
filtration, secretion → add drug to the lumen

segs.text: Glomerular filtration is passive diffusion of drug from the blood across the glomerulus into the tubule, so it needs no energy. In normal kidneys it averages one hundred twenty milliliters per minute. Only unbound drug is filtered, so drug bound to plasma protein stays in the blood. Active tubular secretion uses a transporter and energy to move drug from the blood into the urine, so it removes drug on top of what filtration removes. Tubular reabsorption moves some drug from the urine in the tubule back into the blood, so it takes away from what was removed.

Because of this, a drug's renal clearance, Cl R, compared with one hundred twenty milliliters per minute tells you which processes are at work. Cl R equals filtration plus secretion minus reabsorption, with each term in milliliters per minute. Secretion is apparent when renal clearance is greater than the filtration rate, because secretion is then adding to filtration. This is a reasoning rule, not a line on the equation sheet.

Reabsorption occurs when renal clearance is less than the clearance by filtration. So a value below one hundred twenty milliliters per minute means some filtered drug is returning to the blood, and a value of about one hundred twenty means filtration alone. She allows a margin. She said, I'm saying one hundred twenty. If it's one hundred nineteen, one hundred twenty one let's call that filtration. If it's two hundred fifty, then let's assume that we've got some active secretion going on.

A worked example. A drug has a total body clearance of fifty two point nine five milliliters per minute per seventy kilograms and a renal clearance of thirty four point seven two milliliters per minute per seventy kilograms, and the probable mechanism of its renal clearance is asked. The mechanism is read from renal clearance only, so total clearance is set aside. Both values are already in milliliters per minute, so no conversion is needed. Thirty four point seven two is less than one hundred twenty milliliters per minute. The kidney removes less drug than filtration alone would, so some filtered drug must be returning to the blood. The mechanism is glomerular filtration with tubular reabsorption.

Her own example goes the other way: a renal clearance of three hundred fifty milliliters per minute means filtration plus active secretion. In her questions the stem gives a renal clearance and the answer is the process, with one hundred twenty milliliters per minute as the reference on both sides, so the item tests direction, not arithmetic. A usual trap reads a value below one hundred twenty as reduced filtration; within this rule, a value below the filtration rate points to drug returning to the blood. A second trap compares a renal clearance in liters per hour with one hundred twenty milliliters per minute without converting.
